Egglestone
EG-ul-stun
n. (the small Premonstratensian abbey above the Tees in County Durham, founded c. 1195)
Old English Egleston, Egel's farmstead; unrelated to ecclesia despite the look of the name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Egglestone Abbey stands above the Tees near Barnard Castle, founded about 1195 by Ralph de Multon for Premonstratensian canons — the white canons, an order that lived under a rule stricter than the Augustinians' and served parishes as well as choirs. Egglestone was always small and always poor. Its income was repeatedly reported insufficient, it suffered from Scottish raiding after Bannockburn, and more than once the abbey asked to be reduced in status. At the dissolution in 1540 there were a handful of canons left. The buildings passed into a private house and then into ruin. The dictionary records Egglestone for its smallness, because the medieval system is usually described from its great houses and most of its houses were like this one. A dozen men on a thin income, saying offices above a river, are a better picture of the whole than Fountains or Rievaulx. Scripture neither mocks nor flatters them. “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10) honours the humblest place in God's house, and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) denies that the humility earns anything.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a canon regular as one living under a rule; poverty as want of means; a doorkeeper as one who guards an entrance; humility as freedom from pride; and merit as desert of reward.

expand to see more

CANON, a. (regular) One who lives according to a rule, as distinguished from a secular canon not so bound.

POOR, a. Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence.

DOORKEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.

HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; a modest estimate of one's own worth.

MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.

Key Scripture

Psa 84:10 — "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

Eph 2:9 — "Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Phi 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

Eph 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Modern Corruption

Small, poor Premonstratensian house above the Tees, founded c. 1195 and dissolved in 1540 with only a few canons left.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the lowest place in God's house is a good place and not a meritorious one. The Psalmist chooses it outright, “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10), and the choice is affection rather than accounting. Egglestone's few poor canons occupied something like that place for three and a half centuries.

The live temptation is to let poverty itself do the work of righteousness, which is the error the white canons' rule was always close to. Paul refuses it for himself in the sharpest terms, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), and the alternative he names is a righteousness received. Hence the governing sentence for a poor house and a rich one alike: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew saphaph (H5605), to wait at the threshold; Greek dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; Greek charis (G5485), grace; Greek ergon (G2041), a work.

expand to see more

Hebrew saphaph (H5605) — to wait at the threshold, to be a doorkeeper; “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God”, Psalm 84:10.

Hebrew chatser (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God”, Psalm 84:10.

Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law”, Philippians 3:9.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unmerited favour; “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves”, Ephesians 2:8.

Greek ergon (G2041) — a work, a deed; “Not of works, lest any man should boast.”, Ephesians 2:9.

Usage

"“I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10) — affection, not accounting."

"“not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9) — what poverty cannot manufacture."

"“by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) — the same sentence for a poor house and a rich one."
